plan.contextChunk: This figure looks straight down the axis of a chair-form cyclohexane ring in two matched models that color-code the two kinds of hydrogen position. On the left is a space-filling model: a compact dark gray core of ring carbons is surrounded by six large red spheres and six large blue spheres packed against one another, the red ones sitting toward the center of the disc and the blue ones fanning outward around the rim, the two colors alternating as the eye travels around the ring. A magenta arrow at the upper left points to a red sphere and is labeled "Axial"; a blue arrow at the top points to a blue sphere and is labeled "Equatorial". On the right the same view appears as a ball-and-stick model, the six dark gray carbons forming a hexagonal outline, with red spheres projecting from alternating carbons and blue spheres held outward from every carbon on thin pale rods. Separating the two positions by color rather than by perspective lets the reader count them directly, establishing that each ring carbon bears exactly one axial and one equatorial hydrogen and that each face carries three of each in alternating order.

elements: six dark-gray ring carbon spheres arranged on a circle (alternating +z / -z to form the chair)
six red axial-hydrogen spheres, one per carbon, pointing straight along +z on up-carbons and -z on down-carbons
six light-blue equatorial-hydrogen spheres, one per carbon, fanning radially outward with a slight opposite-z tilt
six C-C bond cylinders forming the puckered hexagonal ring
six C-H(axial) bond cylinders (vertical)
six C-H(equatorial) bond cylinders (outward, pale)
magenta 'Axial' label with arrow pointing to one red sphere
blue 'Equatorial' label with arrow pointing to one blue sphere
faint dashed C3 symmetry axis through the ring center (vertical)

interactions.teaches: Tilting away from the top-down view reveals the puckered chair: axial H's stand parallel to the C3 axis while equatorial H's lie around the rim, explaining why the two positions are geometrically distinct

interactions.label: Model
interactions.teaches: Switching between the two matched representations shows the same axial/equatorial color pattern whether bonds are exposed or atoms are packed, confirming the pattern is intrinsic to the molecule not the drawing style

interactions.label: Hydrogens shown
interactions.teaches: Isolating one color at a time lets the learner count three axial and three equatorial hydrogens per face in alternating order, then see them recombine into one-axial-one-equatorial at every carbon
Clicking any ring carbon brightens its own axial and equatorial hydrogen together, proving the two positions coexist on a single carbon rather than belonging to different molecules

demo_steps.title: Both positions, ball-and-stick
demo_steps.narration: Top-down the chair shows red axial H's clustered near the ring center and blue equatorial H's fanning outward, alternating around the hexagon.

demo_steps.title: Axial only
demo_steps.narration: Hiding the blue leaves three red axial H's on one face pointing up and three on the opposite face pointing down — countable and alternating.

demo_steps.title: Equatorial only
demo_steps.narration: Hiding the red leaves six blue equatorial H's ringing the perimeter, again three per face in alternating order.

demo_steps.title: Space-filling, both
demo_steps.narration: In the packed model the same red-inner / blue-outer alternation appears, matching the textbook's left panel.

demo_steps.title: Select one carbon
demo_steps.narration: Click a gray carbon: its single red axial and single blue equatorial H glow together, showing both positions live on that one atom.

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: Chair cyclohexane centered at origin. Ring carbons on a circle of radius 1.25 in the XY plane at angles 0,60,...,300 deg; up-carbons (0,120,240) at z=+0.30, down-carbons (60,180,300) at z=-0.30. Carbon sphere radius 0.20 (ball-stick) / 0.55 (space-fill), color #444444. Axial H at carbon + (0,0,+0.95) for up-carbons and (0,0,-0.95) for down-carbons, radius 0.13 / 0.45, red #cc2222. Equatorial H direction = normalize(cos(theta), sin(theta), -0.35*sign(z_carbon)) * 1.0 from the carbon, radius 0.13 / 0.45, light blue #4aa3e0. Bonds: C-C pale gray #bbbbbb radius 0.05; C-H bonds radius 0.035 pale #dddddd. C3 axis dashed line along z from -1.6 to +1.6, faint gray. Labels: 'Axial' magenta #cc00aa arrow to the up-carbon axial H at 120 deg; 'Equatorial' blue #1a86d0 arrow to the equatorial H at 90-ish deg. Whole scene spans ~±2.4 in XY and ±1.6 in Z. Default camera top-down (elevation 90) reproduces the source disc view; orbit reveals the chair puckering.
interactionPlan.notes: Build the molecule once as a group; the modelStyle toggle scales atom radii and toggles bond visibility (lerp for a smooth morph). hVisibility fades axial or equatorial atom+bond subgroups via material opacity. selectCarbon raycasts carbon spheres and boosts emissive on that carbon's two H spheres plus its two C-H bonds, dimming others slightly. Keep both label arrows as screen-space sprites anchored to their target atoms so they track orbiting. Use MeshStandardMaterial with a soft key light from above and ambient fill so the space-filling spheres read as glossy like the source.

authoredContext:
As shown in the figure, each carbon atom in chair cyclohexane has one axial and one equatorial hydrogen. Furthermore, each side of the ring has three axial and three equatorial hydrogens in an alternating arrangement. For example, if the top side of the ring has axial hydrogens on carbons 1, 3, and 5, then it has equatorial hydrogens on carbons 2, 4, and 6. The reverse is true for the bottom side: carbons 1, 3, and 5 have equatorial hydrogens, but carbons 2, 4, and 6 have axial hydrogens (the figure).

Alternating axial and equatorial positions in chair cyclohexane, looking directly down the ring axis. Each carbon atom has one axial and one equatorial position, and each face has alternating axial and equatorial positions.

The space-filling model and ball and stick model of cyclohexane with alternate axial and equatorial positions, represented by red and blue spheres, respectively.

Note that we haven’t used the words cis and trans in this discussion of cyclohexane conformation. Two hydrogens on the same side of the ring are always cis, regardless of whether they’re axial or equatorial and regardless of whether they’re adjacent. Similarly, two hydrogens on opposite sides of the ring are always trans.

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: Chair cyclohexane centered at origin. Ring carbons on a circle of radius 1.25 in the XY plane at angles 0,60,...,300 deg; up-carbons (0,120,240) at z=+0.30, down-carbons (60,180,300) at z=-0.30. Carbon sphere radius 0.20 (ball-stick) / 0.55 (space-fill), color #444444. Axial H at carbon + (0,0,+0.95) for up-carbons and (0,0,-0.95) for down-carbons, radius 0.13 / 0.45, red #cc2222. Equatorial H direction = normalize(cos(theta), sin(theta), -0.35*sign(z_carbon)) * 1.0 from the carbon, radius 0.13 / 0.45, light blue #4aa3e0. Bonds: C-C pale gray #bbbbbb radius 0.05; C-H bonds radius 0.035 pale #dddddd. C3 axis dashed line along z from -1.6 to +1.6, faint gray. Labels: 'Axial' magenta #cc00aa arrow to the up-carbon axial H at 120 deg; 'Equatorial' blue #1a86d0 arrow to the equatorial H at 90-ish deg. Whole scene spans ~±2.4 in XY and ±1.6 in Z. Default camera top-down (elevation 90) reproduces the source disc view; orbit reveals the chair puckering.
interactionPlan.notes: Build the molecule once as a group; the modelStyle toggle scales atom radii and toggles bond visibility (lerp for a smooth morph). hVisibility fades axial or equatorial atom+bond subgroups via material opacity. selectCarbon raycasts carbon spheres and boosts emissive on that carbon's two H spheres plus its two C-H bonds, dimming others slightly. Keep both label arrows as screen-space sprites anchored to their target atoms so they track orbiting. Use MeshStandardMaterial with a soft key light from above and ambient fill so the space-filling spheres read as glossy like the source.

plan.authoredPrompt: This figure looks straight down the axis of a chair-form cyclohexane ring in two matched models that color-code the two kinds of hydrogen position. On the left is a space-filling model: a compact dark gray core of ring carbons is surrounded by six large red spheres and six large blue spheres packed against one another, the red ones sitting toward the center of the disc and the blue ones fanning outward around the rim, the two colors alternating as the eye travels around the ring. A magenta arrow at the upper left points to a red sphere and is labeled "Axial"; a blue arrow at the top points to a blue sphere and is labeled "Equatorial". On the right the same view appears as a ball-and-stick model, the six dark gray carbons forming a hexagonal outline, with red spheres projecting from alternating carbons and blue spheres held outward from every carbon on thin pale rods. Separating the two positions by color rather than by perspective lets the reader count them directly, establishing that each ring carbon bears exactly one axial and one equatorial hydrogen and that each face carries three of each in alternating order.
plan.authoredInteractions:
- Click for selecting any ring carbon in the ball-and-stick model; its paired axial and equatorial hydrogens brighten together, clarifying that the two positions coexist on each carbon rather than belonging to separate molecules.
- Toggle axial only, equatorial only, and both: red and blue hydrogens fade in and out on both models, making the one-axial-one-equatorial pattern at every ring carbon countable.
plan.sourcePath: OpenStax Organic Chemistry, chapter 4: Organic Compounds: Cycloalkanes and Their Stereochemistry

discrepancies: Camera views the chair conformation from directly above (along C3 axis), making it appear as a flat hexagon; the source shows a 3/4 perspective view where the chair puckering and 3D axial/equatorial distinction are clearly visible
Axial H atoms (red) are nearly invisible/overlapping with carbons in the top-down view, whereas in the source they clearly project above/below the ring plane

The source has two side-by-side panels (space-filling left, ball-and-stick right); the generated figure uses a toggle, which is acceptable but the default view doesn't match either panel's composition
The 3D chair structure (alternating up/down carbons) is completely hidden in the generated view, losing the key spatial relationship the figure is meant to teach
evaluation.notes: The primitives and colors are correct, and the interactions (model toggle, H visibility, step-through) are pedagogically well-designed, but the top-down camera angle completely flattens the chair conformation into an unrecognizable hexagon, destroying the figure's core purpose of showing 3D axial vs equatorial geometry.
action_items: Change the camera to a 3/4 perspective view (elevation ~25-35°, azimuth ~30-45°) so the chair puckering, axial H's projecting up/down, and equatorial H's fanning outward are all clearly visible, matching the source figure's right panel
Ensure axial H atoms are visually distinct from carbons in the default view by adjusting camera angle rather than relying on top-down perspective
Consider showing both models side-by-side or defaulting to a view that matches the source's ball-and-stick panel composition
plan_action_items: The plan should specify a perspective camera angle that reveals the 3D chair structure (not top-down along C3), as the entire pedagogical value depends on seeing axial H's perpendicular to the ring and equatorial H's in the ring plane
